matched_finding.description: The design section declares this is a 'within-subject design with identifiability and intervention as the independent variables,' but the original studies used strictly between-subjects designs. A within-subject design for this paradigm is fundamentally incompatible with the intervention manipulation: once participants learn about the identifiable victim effect, that knowledge cannot be removed for subsequent conditions. Moreover, seeing all victim types (identifiable, statistical, joint) within the same session introduces demand characteristics and contrast effects that would severely confound the identifiable victim effect being measured. The analysis then uses between-subjects F-tests and t-tests, contradicting the stated within-subject design.
matched_finding.quote: We embedded Studies 1 and 3 of Small et al. (2007) into a single within-subject design with identifiability and intervention as the independent variables; donation and feeling variables as the dependent variables respectively.

matched_finding.description: The procedures section states that 'Participants selected their preferred intervention and identifiability conditions,' meaning participants self-selected into experimental conditions rather than being randomly assigned. This completely invalidates any causal inference about the effect of intervention or identifiability on donation or feelings. The original studies used strict random assignment to between-subjects conditions. Self-selection introduces severe confounding: participants who choose to learn about the identifiable victim effect likely differ systematically from those who do not.
matched_finding.quote: Participants selected their preferred intervention and identifiability conditions.

matched_finding.description: The manuscript states that 'participants who indicated they had prior knowledge of the identifiable victim effect were excluded, as well as those who failed the attention check,' yet the number of participants excluded under each criterion is never reported. The final analysis N=1000 appears to be the initial generated sample, not a post-exclusion count. Pre-registration and replication standards require transparent reporting of how many participants were excluded and for which reasons to evaluate whether exclusions could have influenced results.

The "availability heuristic"  (Tversky & Kahneman, 1973), which relies on the ease of retrieving relevant instances from memory, is believed to be activated whe...
ground_truth.description: Replaced affect heuristic (emotional arousal) with availability heuristic (memory retrieval) — changes the theoretical mechanism; intervention design and feeling measures no longer match the theory

matched_finding.description: The paper attributes the affect-driven component of the identifiable victim effect to the 'availability heuristic' (Tversky & Kahneman, 1973). The availability heuristic concerns ease of mentally retrieving instances and is a frequency/probability judgment heuristic. The mechanism by which identifiable victims elicit more giving is better characterized by the 'affect heuristic' (prominently discussed in Slovic et al., 2007, which is even cited in the references) or affect/imagery mechanisms. Small et al. (2007) themselves frame this as an affective, not availability-based, process. This is a theoretical mischaracterization of the core mechanism under study.
matched_finding.quote: The 'availability heuristic' (Tversky & Kahneman, 1973), which relies on the ease of retrieving relevant instances from memory, is believed to be activated when we value a personalized individual (Small & Loewenstein, 2003). The information we receive about this person may elicit stronger affective reactions such as sympathy and distress.
